THE NEXT TWO LEVELS OF AI ADOPTION https://every.?ev_audience=free


WHAT COMES AFTER ORCHESTRATION? https://every.?ev_audience=free

by Mike Taylor https://every.?ev_audience=free

Midjourney/Every illustration.

----------------------------------------



In June, we published the eight levels of AI adoption https://every.?ev_audience=free, giving people a map of where they are with AI today and what it takes to get to the next level. The map ran from Level 1, where you ask a chatbot a question, to Level 8, where a manager agent runs a team of subagents for you. I expected most readers to find themselves in the bottom half, and most of them did. What I didn’t expect was how quickly the people at the top would reach the end of the map.

Today, most engineers I talk to are running several long-running agents at once and handing the coordination work to an orchestrator. Even nontechnical teams are progressing faster than I thought they would, because the Codex and Claude desktop apps make orchestration much easier for knowledge work. As more people approach the top end of the eight levels we outlined in June, I keep getting asked, “What comes next?” My answer, which I covered in my talk at Thesis: 2027 https://every.?ev_audience=free last week, is simulation: building a model of the world your agents work in, so you can test strategies before reality does.

In the original framework, each level let you hand off longer stretches of work and gave the AI more autonomy, with orchestration representing the most you could hand off. Today, there’s no reason to believe that pattern should end with orchestration. Once you have agents managing and executing the work, the harder question becomes which strategy to bet on. Levels 1–8 increased delegation and autonomy. Levels 9 and 10 extend how agents explore and test strategies. Level 9 pits strategies against each other to find the best one, and Level 10 runs that competition multiple times to see which strategies win consistently.

Here they are, with some caveats: These are firmly in experimental territory and burn many more tokens than lower levels, and as always, working at a higher level doesn’t guarantee better results today—it’s an investment in tomorrow.


THE NEXT TWO LEVELS OF AI ADOPTION

At Level 8, you’ve removed yourself as the bottleneck on a single project. An orchestrator agent takes tasks off your to-do list, hands them to subagents, and escalates only the decisions that need a human. Steve Yegge’s Gas Town https://every.?ev_audience=free, Paperclip, and OpenAI’s Symphony were early examples of orchestration systems, but today most of this is possible directly in the standard AI desktop apps.


LEVEL 9: SIMULATION—MAKE AGENT TEAMS COMPETE ON STRATEGY

https://every.?ev_audience=freeMidjourney/Every illustration.




What it is: At Level 9, you stop designing a system and start designing an ecosystem. Instead of one orchestrator working through one plan, you have several orchestrated teams working toward the same goal, each with its own strategy. The strategies that work survive, and the rest get dropped, much like companies competing within an industry, only faster.

What changes at this level: You move from asking, “What’s the best plan?” to asking, “What’s the best way to find out which plan is best?” Your job becomes defining the goal, the scoring, and the rules of competition and then trusting the competition to find the best plan.

What you can use it for: Problems where you don’t know which approach will work, and trying several at once is cheaper than guessing wrong. Growth experiments, pricing strategy, and content strategy are good candidates, as is any engineering problem that could be solved in more than one way.

An orchestrator manages faceless subagents, which all converge on the same ideas. To build an AI society, you need a diversity of ideas, which means you need to populate it with synthetic people. That’s less far-fetched than it sounds, because we’ve been building a small version of it at Every for the past few months. Dan Lens https://every.?ev_audience=free is a prompt that replies to a Slack thread the way Dan Shipper https://every.?ev_audience=free would, optimized by replaying his past Slack messages and predicting what he would say in that scenario. On 83 threads it hadn’t seen before, Dan Lens’s first guess makes 26 percent of the points Dan actually made, but give it 100 guesses and it covers 86 percent. KatePass does the same for our editor in chief, Kate Lee https://every.?ev_audience=free: My colleague Jannik Jung optimized it from 594 of her editing passes (24,000 individual edits), and on drafts it had never seen, it makes about twice as many of the good edits and a third as many of the harmful ones as the manually written rules-based version it replaced. I’ve also gone a step further and built a synthetic Slack workspace filled with clones of everyone in the company, each distilled from a year of their public Slack messages.

None of these clones are perfect, and that’s partly the point. As Dan put it in his Thesis talk https://every.?ev_audience=free, generation is cheap, but ranking is hard: A single clone can’t tell you which of its guesses is the one he’d actually say. A society of them can argue, push back, and react to each other the way real colleagues do, helping expose weaknesses in each other’s ideas and improve them.

Try it:

Prompt

Using the persona files for each person on our marketing team, set up three synthetic versions of the team, each led by a clone of a different team member and told to plan our product launch their way. Have each team write a launch plan, then put all three in front of a panel of 50 synthetic customers built from our interview transcripts. Score the plans on how many customers say they’d sign up, have the two losing teams critique the winner and revise their plans, and run three rounds. Give me the final winning plan, what changed between rounds, and which objections from the team-member clones never got resolved.




Input: Persona files for the people involved (built from their Slack messages, docs, or meeting transcripts), synthetic customers built from real research, a goal, and a scoring rule.

Output: A launch plan that has survived several rounds of competition and critique, plus a record of which ideas won and why.

Human judgment: Check the winning plan with the real people before you act on it. The clones show what your colleagues might say, not what they will say, so use the society to find the strongest plan and the likely objections, then bring both to the actual meeting.

The limitation: Every team needs its own reliable orchestration, and if a single orchestrator still needs a human watching it, three competing ones need three times the human attention. It also costs many more tokens to run several approaches to find one winner, which only makes sense when picking the wrong strategy would cost you more in time and money than running a real-world experiment would.


LEVEL 10: MULTIVERSE—RERUN THE WORLD TO FILTER OUT CHANCE

https://every.?ev_audience=freeMidjourney/Every illustration.




What it is: At Level 10, you run the same simulation many times to determine how much of the result comes down to chance. If Level 9 is a single competition between strategies, Level 10 is running that competition many times over, with the same starting conditions, to see what wins on average rather than what happened to win once.

A 2006 study https://every.?ev_audience=free by researchers at Columbia University and the Santa Fe Institute shows how much chance can influence which ideas succeed. The study split 14,341 people into eight separate “music worlds,” each with the same 48 songs by unknown bands. When people could see what others in their world were listening to, the same song could be a hit in one world and a flop in another. The best songs rarely flopped, and the worst rarely hit, but almost any other result was possible, because popularity is a dynamic, chaotic system where a few lucky early picks compound.

I ran into the same wall with my Hacker News https://every.?ev_audience=free simulator. I cloned https://every.?ev_audience=free nearly 2,000 Hacker News commenters as AI personas, and they predicted which headlines would make the front page 60 percent of the time. When I dug into the misses, the personas weren’t the problem. One extra early upvote could send identical content down completely different paths in parallel experiments. Even if you model every individual well, you can still be wrong about the outcome. Running many universes and averaging the results lowers the risk of a decision when the system is too complex to predict.

What changes at this level: You stop treating any single result as the answer. A strategy that wins in one universe might just be lucky. A strategy that wins in 40 out of 50 is robust. Spend enough tokens, and you can determine how much of your outcome was luck.

What you can use it for: High-stakes decisions where the outcome depends on how people react to each other, such as product launches, pricing changes, or how a message spreads through a market. Run the same experiment multiple times and see how often one idea wins. You’ll learn what ideas are good and which of your wins are mostly luck, so you can stop trying to repeat them.

Try it:

Prompt

Run our launch simulation 50 times using the same customer personas, but vary the order in which they see the announcement and which early reactions they’re exposed to. For each of our three headline options, report how often it comes out on top, the range of outcomes, and flag any headline that only wins when it gets a lucky start.




Input: A simulation of the system you care about (personas, a market, a feed), the options you’re deciding between, and enough budget to run it many times.

Output: A range of outcomes for each option, so you can see which ones win reliably and which ones need luck.

Human judgment: Decide how much risk you’re willing to accept. A reliable option that wins modestly may be a better bet than a volatile one that occasionally wins big.

The obvious limitation is that the simulation has to be good enough to be worth running 50 times. If the personas or the market model are off, averaging many runs just gives you a very confident wrong answer. The simulation can find you the best option, but reality is the ultimate test. For now, this works best on narrow, well-defined systems like a single social feed or a focus group, and only a handful of teams https://every.?ev_audience=free are doing it at all.


WHEN WILL IT START WORKING FOR YOU?

These levels sound speculative, but they follow logically: Once you’re managing one team of agents, you’ll want to manage multiple, and since they interact, you’ll need to run the simulation multiple times to see how often something works. Each level extends the time horizon and increases the AI’s autonomy, while token prices dropping 90 percent https://every._?ev_audience=free make it possible to trade tokens for quality outputs. If Level 8 is a code factory for one project, Level 9 is multiple factories competing to find the best approach, and Level 10 is running those competitions many times to determine what works on average. Even six months ago, people thought software factories were an outrageous waste of tokens, so these upper levels felt far-fetched. In six more months, maybe we’ll become accustomed to simulation, and a new frontier will open up ahead of us.

The real question is when this will start working for you given your risk tolerance. The answer will be different for an engineer already bumping up against Level 8 than for an operator who just got comfortable at Level 3 and can safely ignore this post (for now). As with the first eight levels, the goal isn’t to climb as high as you can for the sake of it but to know what’s possible at each stage so you can recognize when the economics finally tip in your favor.
